hero.title: Financial Wellness Programs for Employees
hero.subtitle: Helping employees build stronger financial habits today so they can prepare more confidently for retirement.

blocks.text: Financial stress doesn't stay outside the workplace. When employees are struggling with debt, emergency savings, or day-to-day cash flow, long-term retirement planning often takes a back seat. PointOak develops financial wellness programs that address those immediate challenges while connecting better financial habits to stronger retirement outcomes.

items: Programs designed around your workforce and retirement plan

sections.title: The Benefits of Financial Wellness Programs

body.text: Money worries can affect focus, productivity, and overall employee wellbeing. Financial wellness programs give employees practical guidance for managing the issues creating that stress, from budgeting and debt to savings and long-term planning.

Employees who are struggling to meet today's financial obligations are less likely to increase retirement contributions tomorrow. By helping participants establish emergency savings, manage debt, and improve cash flow, we create a stronger foundation for long-term retirement planning.

Information alone doesn't always change behavior. We help employees understand their options and put that knowledge into practice, giving them greater confidence in the decisions they make about saving, investing, and preparing for the future.

Financial wellness extends the value of your retirement plan beyond an account balance. Providing employees with practical financial support demonstrates an investment in their overall financial health and can strengthen the value of your broader benefits package.

A successful financial wellness program should do more than generate webinar attendance. We help plan sponsors look at engagement, savings behavior, participation, and other plan-level indicators to understand whether the program is helping employees take action.

sections.title: Who Benefits Most from Financial Wellness Programs?

body.text: If employees are enrolled but contribution rates aren't increasing, broader financial pressures may be keeping them from saving more. Financial wellness can help address the issues preventing stronger retirement participation.

items.title: Employees Aren't Engaging With Existing Resources

body.text: Your recordkeeper may already offer calculators, articles, and webinars. If employees aren't using them, the issue may be relevance rather than availability. Customized programs connect financial education to the real questions your workforce is asking.

items.title: Financial Stress Is Affecting Your Workforce

body.text: Employees dealing with debt, insufficient emergency savings, or cash-flow challenges may need support before they can focus meaningfully on retirement.

Early-career employees, mid-career professionals, and those approaching retirement have very different financial concerns. A customized financial wellness strategy allows you to address each stage appropriately.

items.title: You Want Financial Wellness to Support Your Retirement Plan

body.text: Financial wellness works best when it isn't treated as an unrelated perk. We connect the program to your plan design, employee education, and broader retirement readiness goals.

items.title: When a Broader Financial Wellness Program May Not Be Necessary

body.text: If participation is strong, employees actively use existing educational resources, and your workforce has relatively straightforward financial needs, a more focused retirement education program may be enough.

sections.title: Financial Wellness vs. Retirement Education Alone

blocks.text: Both have a role. Retirement education focuses specifically on helping employees understand and use their retirement benefits. Financial wellness looks at the broader financial issues that can affect their ability to do so.
For many employers, the strongest approach combines both: helping employees manage their financial lives while also giving them the knowledge they need to make the most of their retirement plan.

body.text: We review your existing benefits, retirement plan engagement, and areas where employees may need additional financial support.
We determine which topics and workforce segments would benefit most from targeted education and guidance.
Your financial wellness strategy is customized around your workforce, plan design, and organizational goals rather than pulled from a generic content library.
Programs may include group education, webinars, communication campaigns, and individualized guidance depending on your needs.

items.title: Financial Wellness Connected to Retirement Outcomes

body.text: PointOak isn't a standalone financial wellness vendor. We're retirement plan specialists.

We've worked with plan sponsors and participants since 2005, giving us a clear understanding of how day-to-day financial decisions ultimately affect retirement readiness. That allows us to connect financial wellness directly to your existing retirement plan rather than treating it as a separate employee perk.

As an independent, fee-only fiduciary, our guidance isn't influenced by product sales or recordkeeper relationships. We focus on providing useful, understandable financial education designed around your employees and your organization's goals.

items.q: What is a financial wellness program?

a.text: A financial wellness program helps employees strengthen their overall financial health through education, tools, and guidance.

Programs may address budgeting, debt, emergency savings, retirement planning, and other everyday financial decisions. The goal is to help employees feel more confident managing their finances while removing some of the barriers that can prevent long-term saving.

items.q: What's the difference between financial education and financial coaching?

a.text: Financial education teaches concepts, while coaching helps employees apply those concepts to their individual circumstances.

Education may include workshops, webinars, or group sessions covering topics such as budgeting and saving. More personalized guidance helps participants translate what they've learned into practical financial decisions.

items.q: How do financial wellness programs support retirement planning?

a.text: They address many of the financial pressures that compete with retirement saving.

Employees dealing with debt, cash-flow shortages, or insufficient emergency savings may be reluctant to increase retirement contributions. Helping them strengthen those areas can make it easier to engage with their employer-sponsored retirement plan.

items.q: Do employees actually use financial wellness programs?

a.text: Engagement depends heavily on how relevant and accessible the program is.

Generic resources can be easy to ignore. Programs built around real employee concerns and delivered at meaningful moments—such as enrollment, major plan changes, or financial milestones—give employees a clearer reason to participate.

items.q: What should a financial wellness program include?

a.text: The right mix depends on your workforce.

Common areas include budgeting, debt management, emergency savings, retirement contributions, and personalized financial guidance. The program should be built around the actual needs of employees rather than offering every possible financial topic.

items.q: How is financial wellness different from employee retirement education?

a.text: Retirement education focuses specifically on the retirement plan. Financial wellness addresses the broader financial picture that affects an employee's ability to save for retirement.

The two services work particularly well together: financial wellness strengthens the foundation, while retirement education helps participants make better use of the benefits your organization provides.
